claim: TCRs are formed by stochastic gene rearrangements, theoretically generating >10^19 sequences.
source: T-cell receptors (TCRs) are formed by stochastic gene rearrangements, theoretically generating >1019 sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of TCR generation.

claim: Thymopoiesis releases a repertoire of about 10^8 unique TCRs per individual.
source: They are selected during thymopoiesis, which releases a repertoire of about 108 unique TCRs per individual.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Human thymopoiesis releases a large population of clustered CD8+ T cells harboring α/β paired TCRs that have high generation probabilities.
source: We show here that human thymopoiesis releases a large population of clustered CD8+ T cells harboring α/β paired TCRs that (i) have high generation probabilities
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Clustered CD8+ T cells show preferential usage of some V and J genes.
source: We show here that human thymopoiesis releases a large population of clustered CD8+ T cells harboring α/β paired TCRs that (i) have high generation probabilities and (ii) a preferential usage of some V and J genes
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3G and H.

claim: CDR3s of clustered CD8+ T cells are shared between individuals.
source: We show here that human thymopoiesis releases a large population of clustered CD8+ T cells harboring α/β paired TCRs that (i) have high generation probabilities and (ii) a preferential usage of some V and J genes, (iii) which CDR3 are shared between individuals
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2A and Figure 2D.

claim: Polyspecific TCRs can each bind and be activated by multiple unrelated viral peptides, notably from EBV, CMV, and influenza.
source: We show here that human thymopoiesis releases a large population of clustered CD8+ T cells harboring α/β paired TCRs that (i) have high generation probabilities and (ii) a preferential usage of some V and J genes, (iii) which CDR3 are shared between individuals, and (iv) can each bind and be activated by multiple unrelated viral peptides, notably from EBV, CMV, and influenza.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of clustered βCDR3s from DPCD3− to CD8+ thymocytes (p<0.0001).
source: We observed a significant increase in the number of clustered βCDR3s from DPCD3− to CD8+ thymocytes (Figure 1A and B) (p<0.0001)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The degree of clustered CDR3s is significantly increased during T-cell differentiation for clustered βCDR3s (p<0.0001).
source: The degree of clustered CDR3s, that is, the number of neighbors based on LD≤1, was also significantly increased during T-cell differentiation for clustered βCDR3s (Figure 1C and D) (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Clustered TCRs from both DPCD3+ and CD8+ thymocytes have a significantly higher Pgen (p<0.0001) than the dispersed ones.
source: We evaluated the generation probability (Pgen) of each CDR3 pre- and post-selection (Sethna et al., 2019): (i) clustered TCRs from both DPCD3+ and CD8+ thymocytes have a significantly higher Pgen (p<0.0001) than the dispersed ones (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to the Pgen calculation method and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Pgen increased significantly (p<0.0001) from DPCD3+ to CD8+ thymocytes.
source: (ii) Pgen increased significantly (p<0.0001) from DPCD3+ to CD8+ thymocytes (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is a robust correlation between βCDR3 Pgen and their number of connections (p<0.0001).
source: (iii) there is a robust correlation between βCDR3 Pgen and their number of connections (p<0.0001) (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Clustered βCDR3s belong to TCRs that have a preferential usage of V and J genes, with a significant (p<0.01) overrepresentation of Vβ 12-3, 27, 5-1, and 7-9 and of JB 1-1 and 2-7.
source: Clustered βCDR3s belong to TCRs that have a preferential usage of V and J genes, with a significant (p<0.01) overrepresentation of Vβ 12-3, 27, 5-1, and 7-9 and of JB 1-1 and 2-7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G and H.

claim: Clustered βCDR3s are enriched in public sequences (p<0.0001).
source: Clustered βCDR3s are also enriched in public sequences, that is, being shared between at least two individuals (p<0.0001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a significant increase of public βCDR3s in CD8+ versus DPCD3+ thymocytes (p<0.0001).
source: The significant increase of public βCDR3s in CD8+ versus DPCD3+ thymocytes (p<0.0001) is mostly that of the clustered βCDR3s.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support.

claim: Up to 31.7% of clustered βCDR3s in CD8+ thymocytes are public compared to barely 1% of the dispersed ones.
source: For CD8+ thymocytes, up to 31.7% of clustered βCDR3s are public compared to barely 1% of the dispersed ones (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Public βCDR3 have a significantly higher Pgen than the private ones (p<0.0001).
source: Public βCDR3 have a significantly higher Pgen than the private ones (p<0.0001) (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of public βCDR3 shared between individuals is independent of the number of shared HLA Class I alleles.
source: Noteworthy, the number of public βCDR3 shared between individuals is independent of the number of shared HLA Class I alleles (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Virus-specific βCDR3s are enriched in clustered versus dispersed CD8+ thymocytes (p<0.0001).
source: We detected an enrichment of these virus-specific βCDR3s in clustered versus dispersed CD8+ thymocytes (p<0.0001)
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support.

claim: Virus-specific βCDR3s are enriched in CD8+ versus DPCD3+ thymocytes (p<0.0001).
source: We detected an enrichment of these virus-specific βCDR3s in clustered versus dispersed CD8+ thymocytes (p<0.0001) and in CD8+ versus DPCD3+ thymocytes (p<0.0001) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical support shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Virus-specific βCDR3s were significantly enriched in βCDR3s with the highest Pgen and number of connections.
source: Moreover, these virus-specific βCDR3s were significantly enriched in βCDR3s with the highest Pgen and number of connections (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Virus-associated CDR3s amounted to up to 7.4% and 12.3% of the DPCD3+ and CD8+ cells CDR3 repertoires, respectively.
source: In the latter representation, the 13,557 connected CDR3s (i) covered most of the clustered CDR3s of all individuals (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), (ii) amounted to up to 7.4% and 12.3% of the DPCD3+ and CD8+ cells CDR3 repertoires, respectively (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Among the 13,557 virus-associated βCDR3s, almost 7% (958/13557) are in silico assigned (LD≤1) as specific for at least two distinct viruses.
source: In addition, among the 13,557 virus-associated βCDR3s that we previously estimated in CD8+ thymocytes (Figure 3E, 'LD≤1'), almost 7% (958/13557) are in silico assigned (LD≤1) as specific for at least two distinct viruses (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: GLIPH2 identified 93,182 specificity groups from 216,000 CDR3β sequences from CD8+ thymocytes and 32,496 tetramer-specific sequences.
source: The GLIPH2 algorithm groups together CDR3s that have structural characteristics that make them likely to recognize the same antigens, hence called 'specificity groups' (Glanville et al., 2017). GLIPH2 identified 93,182 such specificity groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to the GLIPH2 algorithm.

claim: 31.6% of GLIPH2 specificity groups contained at least one CDR3 with a known viral specificity.
source: Noteworthy, 31.6% of these specificity groups contained at least one CDR3 with a known viral specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 6.8% of GLIPH2 specificity groups contained CDR3s with more than one specificity, and up to nine different ones.
source: Even more surprisingly, 6.8% of GLIPH2 specificity groups contained CDR3s with more than one specificity, and up to nine different ones (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Single cells harboring TCRs can bind to multiple dextramers presenting different unrelated peptides.
source: We could identify numerous single cells harboring TCRs that did bind to multiple dextramers, which others also observed but excluded from their analysis (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation and supported by data in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Almost all of 2074 cells using the same CASSIRSSYEQYF βCDR3 had the highest binding score for a matched HLA-A*0201 dextramer bound to an influenza peptide.
source: Almost all of these 2074 cells had the highest binding score for a matched HLA-A*0201 dextramer bound to an influenza peptide, indicating that the strong binding of this dextramer was mostly driven by this βCDR3.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Approximately half of 2074 cells using CASSIRSSYEQYF βCDR3 also had a noticeable but weaker binding score for three HLA-A*0301 and two A*1101 dextramers presenting peptides from either CMV or EBV.
source: However, approximately half of these 2074 cells also had a noticeable but weaker binding score for the three HLA-A*0301 and two A*1101 dextramers presenting peptides from either CMV or EBV.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Dextramer-sorted cells could be activated by their cognate peptide and almost as well if not better by other unrelated peptides.
source: In contrast, dextramer-sorted cells could be activated by their cognate peptide and almost as well if not better by the other (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Over 85% of CD8+ T cells selected through 18 days of stimulation with pp65 protein peptides produced IFNγ upon stimulation by their cognate peptides.
source: Upon stimulation by their cognate peptides, over 85% of the CD8+ T cells produced IFNγ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A large fraction of CMV pp65-selected T cells produced interferon upon stimulation with a peptide pool covering the BZLF-1 protein of EBV.
source: Surprisingly, a small fraction of the same cells produced interferon upon stimulation with unrelated CMV-IE1 peptides, and a large fraction upon stimulation with a peptide pool which covers the sequence of the BZLF-1 protein of EBV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TCR#35–13 responded strongly to HLA-A*02:01 loaded with Flu MP 58–66 (EC50: 2.02×10–9 M) and CMV IE1-184-192 (EC50: 7.99×10–7 M), and poorly to EBV BMLF1 280–288 (EC50: 9.37×10–3 M).
source: TCR#35–13 responded strongly to HLA-A*02:01 loaded with Flu MP 58–66 (EC50: 2.02×10–9 M) and CMV IE1-184-192 (EC50: 7.99×10–7 M), and poorly to EBV BMLF1 280–288 (EC50: 9.37×10–3 M) (Figure 5C, upper left).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TCR#36–150 had very similar responses for HLA-A*02:01 loaded with Flu MP 58–66 (EC50: 9.99×10–11 M), CMV IE1-184-192 (EC50: 7.99×10–7 M), and EBV BMLF1 280–288 (EC50: 9.37×10–3 M).
source: TCR#36–150 had very similar responses for HLA-A*02:01 loaded with Flu MP 58–66 (EC50: 9.99×10–11 M), CMV IE1-184-192 (EC50: 7.99×10–7 M), and EBV BMLF1 280–288 (EC50: 9.37×10–3 M) (Figure 5C, bottom left).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A control D222D TCR known as specific for a ZnT8 186–194 peptide responded to this peptide (EC50: 2.68×10–7 M), but not to the Flu, EBV, or CMV peptides.
source: In contrast, a control D222D TCR (Culina et al., 2018) known as specific for a ZnT8 186–194 peptide responded to this peptide (EC50: 2.68×10–7 M), but not to the Flu, EBV, or CMV peptides (Figure 5C, upper right).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation and data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A TCR identified as responding to the VMNILLQYV peptide from the Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase protein responded even better to the structurally unrelated SLYNPAIVYA peptide from human chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 2.
source: For example, a TCR identified as responding to the VMNILLQYV peptide from the Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase protein responded even better to the structurally unrelated SLYNPAIVYA peptide from human chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Within the 40,939 curated βCDR3, 24% were from TCRs that could bind at least two totally unrelated viral peptides.
source: Within the 40,939 curated βCDR3, 24% were from TCRs that could bind at least two totally unrelated viral peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on curation of public databases.

claim: A child with an X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency who had a reverse mutation in a single T-cell progenitor was protected from infections despite having a very restricted repertoire of only about 1000 different TCRs.
source: First, a child with an X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency who had a reverse mutation in a single T-cell progenitor was protected from infections despite having a very restricted repertoire of only about 1000 different TCRs (Bousso et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Memory T cells that are specific for one virus can become activated during infection with an unrelated virus.
source: Likewise, for example, (i) memory T cells that are specific for one virus can become activated during infection with an unrelated virus (Verhoeven et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: There are numerous virus-specific memory phenotype T cells in unexposed individuals.
source: (ii) there are numerous virus-specific memory phenotype T cells in unexposed individuals (Su et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: CMV infection enhances the immune response to influenza.
source: (iii) CMV infection enhances the immune response to influenza (Furman et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Tumor-resident memory HBV-specific T-cell responses correlate with hepatocellular carcinoma outcome.
source: (iv) tumor-resident memory HBV-specific T-cell responses correlate with hepatocellular carcinoma outcome (Cheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Each rearrangement has its probability of generation, which has been modeled to vary by about 10 orders of magnitude for the beta chain alone.
source: Each rearrangement has its probability of generation, which has been modeled to vary by about 10 orders of magnitude for the beta chain alone (Bradley and Thomas, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: During their development within the thymus, T cells undergo a selection largely based on the strength of their activation by thymic antigen-presenting cells that eliminates >80% of them.
source: During their development within the thymus, T cells undergo a selection largely based on the strength of their activation by thymic antigen-presenting cells that eliminates >80% of them (Klein et al., 2014; Sinclair et al., 2013; Vrisekoop et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: For each individual, thymopoiesis releases a pool of T cells expressing a repertoire of approximately 10^8 unique TCRs.
source: For each individual, this process releases a pool of T cells expressing a repertoire of approximately 108 unique TCRs (Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: LD≤1 connected CDR3s have been described to most often bind the same peptide.
source: LD≤1 connected CDR3s have been described to most often bind the same peptide (Dash et al., 2017; Klinger et al., 2015; Madi et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017; Qi et al., 2016; Meysman et al., 2019, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: The increase in clustered βCDR3s during thymopoiesis was remarkably consistent among all individuals studied, independently of their age, sex, or HLA.
source: We observed a significant increase in the number of clustered βCDR3s from DPCD3− to CD8+ thymocytes (Figure 1A and B) (p<0.0001), which was remarkably consistent among all individuals studied, independently of their age, sex, or HLA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in the mean Pgen between clustered and dispersed TCRs is of about 20-fold.
source: However, it should be emphasized that the difference in the mean Pgen between clustered and dispersed TCRs is of about 20-fold, which is small when compared to the 10−log10 span of the Pgen of the two populations.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the data.

claim: Many CDR3s with high Pgen do not cluster, indicating that a high Pgen is not the only nor most important driver of clustering.
source: Likewise, many CDR3s with high Pgen do not cluster, indicating that a high Pgen is not the only nor most important driver of clustering (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and F.

claim: There is a clear separation of clustered versus dispersed TCRs in a principal component analysis (PCA) of VJ usages.
source: This results in a clear separation of clustered versus dispersed TCRs in a principal component analysis (PCA) of VJ usages (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A high positive correlation was observed between Pgen and the number of connections, and between cross-individual sharing and the number of connections.
source: Moreover, a high positive correlation was observed between Pgen and the number of connections, and between cross-individual sharing and the number of connections, and to a lesser extent between Pgen and cross-individual sharing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Clustered βCDR3s of one individual can be connected to those of other individuals (up to 12), and more frequently in CD8+ versus DPCD3+ thymocytes.
source: Finally, clustered βCDR3s of one individual can be connected to those of other individuals (up to 12), and more frequently in CD8+ versus DPCD3+ thymocytes (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The mechanisms for TCR generation and for their further thymic selection are biased to shape a public repertoire of connected βCDR3s with shared recognition properties.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the mechanisms for TCR generation and for their further thymic selection are biased to shape a public repertoire of connected βCDR3s with shared recognition properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the data presented.

claim: Virus-specific βCDR3s were highly shared between individuals.
source: Moreover, these virus-specific βCDR3s were significantly enriched in βCDR3s with the highest Pgen and number of connections (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1). They were also highly shared between individuals (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Virus-specific βCDR3s contained a high representation of CMV, EBV, and influenza specificities.
source: They were also highly shared between individuals (Figure 3D) and they contained a high representation of CMV, EBV, and influenza specificities (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 13,557 connected virus-associated CDR3s were highly shared between individuals.
source: In the latter representation, the 13,557 connected CDR3s (i) covered most of the clustered CDR3s of all individuals (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), (ii) amounted to up to 7.4% and 12.3% of the DPCD3+ and CD8+ cells CDR3 repertoires, respectively (Figure 3F), and (iii) were highly shared between individuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The selection of clustered CDR3s with high generation probabilities and high inter-individual sharing corresponds, at least in part, to the selection of virus-specific TCRs whose CDR3s are remarkably conserved between individuals independently of their HLA restriction.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the selection of clustered CDR3s with high generation probabilities and high inter-individual sharing corresponds, at least in part, to the selection of virus-specific TCRs whose CDR3s are remarkably conserved between individuals independently of their HLA restriction and form what could be referred to as a 'paratopic network'.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the data presented.

claim: An in-silico estimation indicated over 10% of the CD8+ thymocytes' TCR repertoire as specific for the small set of 30 tested peptides derived from seven viruses.
source: After thymic selection, an in-silico estimation indicated over 10% of the CD8+ thymocytes' TCR repertoire as specific for the small set of 30 tested peptides derived from seven viruses that was used for the analysis (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A single cluster of βCDR3s from CD8 thymocytes could comprise unique βCDR3s from TCRs that had been assigned to different viral specificities in independent experiments.
source: Actually, we observed that a single cluster of βCDR3s from CD8 thymocytes could comprise unique βCDR3s from TCRs that had been assigned to different viral specificities in independent experiments, for example, to CMV, influenza, EBV, and yellow fever virus (YFV).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the data.

claim: Numerous single CDR3s had been assigned to multiple specificities in public databases of virus-specific TCRs.
source: We explored the public databases of virus-specific TCRs (Tickotsky et al., 2017; Shugay et al., 2018) in more detail and discovered that numerous single CDR3s had been assigned to multiple specificities, for example, single CDR3s binding both CMV and influenza tetramers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: GLIPH2 identified among CD8+ thymocytes' TCRs a large number of clusters with viral specificities, among which a significant fraction appeared polyspecific.
source: Thus, GLIPH2 identified among CD8+ thymocytes' TCRs a large number of clusters with viral specificities, among which a significant fraction appeared polyspecific.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on GLIPH2 analysis.

claim: Single-cell derived TCRs that bind HLA-matched dextramers loaded with EBV or CMV peptides include cells bound to both CMV and EBV dextramers.
source: For example, single-cell derived TCRs that bind HLA-matched dextramers loaded with EBV or CMV peptides are shown (Figure 4B). Projecting the binding of EBV dextramers onto a t-SNE representation based on single-cell specificity identified a few distinct regions that contained CMV (blue) and EBV positive cells (red), and also cells bound to both CMV and EBV dextramers (violet).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A large proportion of the TCRs that bind to the RAKFKQLL peptide also bind the other EBV peptides.
source: As another example, a chord diagram representation of the binding of unique TCRs to HLA-matched EBV dextramers loaded with different EBV peptides (Figure 4C, in green) shows that a large proportion of the TCRs that bind to the RAKFKQLL peptide also bind the other EBV peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Some TCRs recognizing the RAKFKQLL peptide can also bind peptides from CMV, HIV, or Flu.
source: Furthermore, some TCRs recognizing this RAKFKQLL peptide can also bind peptides from CMV (red), HIV (dark blue), or Flu (dark gray) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Each of the five dextramers (three HLA-A*0301 and two A*1101) had their own unique binding patterns, resulting in TCRs that could bind only one of these dextramers to TCRs binding them all or none.
source: Importantly, each of these five dextramers had their own unique binding patterns, resulting in TCRs that could bind only one of these dextramers to TCRs binding them all or none.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the data.

claim: The binding intensity for weak binders is statistically lower when the cells also bind a strong binder.
source: In addition, we observed that the binding intensity for weak binders is statistically lower when the cells also bind a strong binder (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicating that the weak bindings are competed for by strong ones.
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The peptide and HLA-dependent nature of the weak bindings and their competition by strong binders indicate that they are TCR mediated.
source: Altogether, the peptide and HLA-dependent nature of the weak bindings and their competition by strong binders indicate that they are TCR mediated.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the data presented.

claim: There was much fewer KIR+ cells than there were polyspecific ones and there was no association between KIR expression and polyspecificity.
source: There was much fewer KIR+ cells than there were polyspecific ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C) and there was no association between KIR expression and polyspecificity.
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Weak binding patterns could not be linked to the CD45 RA naïve/quiescent versus CD45 RO memory/activated phenotype of the cells, nor to any other relevant genes.
source: Additionally, we showed that these weak binding patterns could not be linked to the CD45 RA naïve/quiescent versus CD45 RO memory/activated phenotype of the cells, nor to any other relevant genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Beside a 'prime' dextramer binding, some 'polyspecific' TCRs can bind weakly to additional dextramers.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that beside a 'prime' dextramer binding, presumably identifying their main specificity, some 'polyspecific' TCRs can bind weakly to additional dextramers.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the data presented.

claim: All T cells were efficiently nonspecifically activated by PMA/ionomycin.
source: All T cells were efficiently nonspecifically activated by PMA/ionomycin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the functional assay.

claim: Control T cells that did not bind CMV nor EBV dextramers could not be stimulated by related peptides.
source: Control T cells that did not bind CMV nor EBV dextramers could not be stimulated by related peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the functional assay.

claim: A small fraction of CMV pp65-selected cells produced interferon upon stimulation with unrelated CMV-IE1 peptides.
source: Surprisingly, a small fraction of the same cells produced interferon upon stimulation with unrelated CMV-IE1 peptides, and a large fraction upon stimulation with a peptide pool which covers the sequence of the BZLF-1 protein of EBV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no interferon production upon stimulation of CMV pp65-selected cells by a peptide pool which covers the EBNA1 protein of EBV.
source: There was no interferon production upon stimulation of the same cells by a peptide pool which covers the EBNA1 protein of EBV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The stimulation with EBV peptides requires a 100-fold higher but still physiological concentration of peptides.
source: The stimulation with EBV peptides requires a 100-fold higher but still physiological concentration of peptides (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: None of the TCRs (TCR#35–13 and TCR#36–150) responded to peptide-pulsed K562 expressing HLA-A*03:01.
source: None of the TCRs responded to peptide-pulsed K562 expressing HLA-A*03:01.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the TCR re-expression experiment.

claim: TCRs derived from single-sorted CD8+ T cells stained with tetramers loaded with pancreatic self-peptides showed marked polyspecificity.
source: We then further analyzed TCRs derived from single-sorted CD8+ T cells stained with tetramers loaded with pancreatic self-peptides. TCRs with known specificities were also cloned and expressed in the reporter cell line. We analyzed their response to a set of peptides comprising their cognate peptide and peptides with no significant structural commonalities, selected by testing combinatorial peptide libraries (Mann et al., 2020). We also observed a marked polyspecificity of these TCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation and data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In a simple curation of public data sets of antiviral TCRs, 24% of the 40,939 curated βCDR3 were from TCRs that could bind at least two totally unrelated viral peptides.
source: In a simple curation of public data sets of antiviral TCRs that were assigned to respond to known viruses—retaining only those from cells that could bind or respond to a known peptide—we found a surprisingly frequent representation of CDR3s that had been assigned to different viral specificities from independent experiments. Within the 40,939 curated βCDR3, 24% were from TCRs that could bind at least two totally unrelated viral peptides.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on curation of public databases.

claim: In dextramer experiments from single-cell sequencing data sets, a single cell could bind multiple dextramers (sometimes a dozen).
source: Noteworthy, in these latter experiments, cells are co-incubated with multiple dextramers bearing a large set of unrelated peptides; although this data set has been widely analyzed, researchers have missed (or dismissed) that a single cell could bind multiple dextramers (sometimes a dozen) possibly because some of these bindings are weak.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from public single-cell data.

claim: There is competition between dextramers for binding at the cell surface during their co-incubation.
source: Furthermore, as there are limited numbers of HLA molecules available per cell, there is competition between dextramers for binding at the cell surface during their co-incubation. We actually observed such competition in which dextramers with weak bindings are competed for by those with strong ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Multiple binding of a single cell to dextramers bearing unrelated peptides indicates multiple specificities.
source: That a single cell binds multiple dextramers bearing unrelated peptides is in our view meaningful. As the binding of multimeric HLA/peptide complexes is a paradigmatic method to define specificity, multiple binding indicates multiple specificities.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The polyspecific nature of TCRs translates in polyreactivity as cloned polyspecific TCRs trigger cell activation in response to multiple peptides.
source: The polyspecific nature of these TCRs translates in polyreactivity as we show here that cloned polyspecific TCRs indeed trigger cell activation in response to multiple peptides, although with different efficiencies and with not always a correlation between the dextramer binding and its reactivity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the functional data presented.

claim: Two cloned TCRs with beta CD3s differing by 2AA and associated with different alpha CDR3s have a remarkably quantitatively similar activation profile for three different unrelated peptides.
source: In this line, two cloned TCRs with beta CD3s differing by 2AA and associated with different alpha CDR3s have a remarkably quantitatively similar activation profile for three different unrelated peptides (Figure 4E), highlighting the assay robustness.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Figure 4E (likely meant to be Figure 5C based on context).

claim: Some peptides that could not properly bind HLA were nevertheless capable of eliciting efficient CD8+ effector T-cell responses capable of eradicating tumors expressing the cognate antigen.
source: In contrast, it has been reported that some peptides that could not properly bind HLA were nevertheless capable of eliciting efficient CD8+ effector T-cell responses capable of eradicating tumors expressing the cognate antigen (Ebrahimi-Nik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to support the claim.

claim: The TCR avidity threshold for functional responses is notoriously lower than that required for dextramer binding.
source: Moreover, it is known that the TCR avidity threshold for functional responses is notoriously lower than that required for dextramer binding (Rius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to support the claim.

claim: T-cell activation results are more relevant for discussing TCR reactivity than dextramer binding.
source: Altogether, this indicates that T-cell activation results are more relevant for discussing TCR reactivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the observations presented.

claim: The polyspecificity of TCRs translates in a polyreactivity of the T cells expressing them, although at peptide concentrations that can span >6 log10 but that are considered physiological.
source: Also, the polyspecificity of TCRs translate in a polyreactivity of the T cells expressing them, although at peptide concentrations that can span >6 log10 but that are considered physiological (Rius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to support the claim.

claim: Each TCR could potentially recognize >10^6 different peptide/MHC combinations.
source: TCRs are notoriously 'cross-reactive', and it is estimated that each TCR could potentially recognize >106 different peptide/MHC combinations (Adams et al., 2016; Birnbaum et al., 2014; Mason, 1998; Wooldridge et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Peptides need to share only five residues at specific positions to bind the same TCR.
source: Also, it was recently shown that peptides need to share only five residues at specific positions to bind the same TCR (Wooldridge et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Bacterial-derived peptides sharing five residues with a tissue-restricted MOG self-antigen can activate a known MOG-specific TCR as well as a MOG peptide.
source: This latter observation has functional relevance as bacterial-derived peptides sharing such five residues with a tissue-restricted MOG self-antigen were shown (i) to activate a known MOG-specific TCR as well as a MOG peptide and (ii) to trigger an autoimmune attack against brain tissues upon mouse immunization (Nelson et al., 2015; Wucherpfennig and Strominger, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: A large part of cross-reactivity is explained by a structural conservation of the TCR interaction surface by different peptides.
source: Thus, a large part of cross-reactivity is explained by a structural conservation of the TCR interaction surface by different peptides (Birnbaum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to support the claim.

claim: According to Don Mason's estimates, each TCR may respond to over 10^6 different peptides from an estimated repertoire of >10^10 possible peptides, making the chance to find a cross-reactive peptide at random around 10^-4.
source: According to Don Mason's estimates, each TCR may respond to over 106 different peptides from an estimated repertoire of >1010 possible peptides, making the chance to find a cross-reactive peptide at random around 10–4.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Don Mason's estimates.

claim: The chance to find even just one cross-reactive peptide among the few peptides tested would be around 10^-3, the chance to find two cross-reactive peptides around 10^-6 and to find three or more cross-reactive peptides infinitesimal.
source: Here, the chance to find even just one cross-reactive peptide among these few peptides that we tested would be around 10–3, the chance to find two cross-reactive peptides around 10–6 and to find three or more cross-reactive peptides infinitesimal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a calculation based on the data.

claim: If the polyreactivity described is part of general cross-reactivity, the results highlight a major previously unreported bias in the selection of these TCRs.
source: Thus, if the polyreactivity that we described is part of this general cross-reactivity, our results are at least highlighting a major previously unreported bias in the selection of these TCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Polyspecificity defines a fuzziness in TCR recognition that makes it capable of interacting with multiple unrelated peptides and that is not strictly HLA-restricted.
source: Thus, polyspecificity appears to have the properties of what was described above as 'degenerate recognition of non-homologous peptides' (Birnbaum et al., 2014). We prefer to describe polyspecificity as defining a fuzziness (rather than 'degeneration') in TCR recognition that makes it capable of interacting with multiple unrelated peptides and that is not strictly HLA-restricted.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: B cells have a machinery for somatic mutations of their BCRs that ultimately allows them to generate antibodies with increased affinity for antigens.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that B cells have a machinery for somatic mutations of their BCRs that ultimately allows them to generate antibodies with increased affinity (specificity) for antigens.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: The fact that T cells did not evolve to use somatic mutations suggests that T-cell recognition may have been selected to be more fuzzy than stringent.
source: While TCR generation and BCR generation share many common mechanisms, the fact that T cells did not evolve to use such somatic mutations suggest that T-cell recognition may have been selected to be more fuzzy than stringent.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: A single cell does not bind randomly to any homologous-HLA/peptide complexes.
source: However, it should be emphasized that a single cell does not bind randomly to any homologous-HLA/peptide complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each polyspecific TCR has its own binding pattern regarding a large set of dextramers, with most that do not bind.
source: Indeed, each polyspecific TCR has its own binding pattern regarding a large set of dextramers, with most that do not bind. Thus, this binding is not just 'nonspecific' and must obey some structural rules that remain to be defined.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: Polyspecific TCR binding properties are distinct from those of innate-like MAIT and NKT cells.
source: Polyspecific TCR binding properties are distinct from those of innate-like MAIT and NKT cells (Toubal et al., 2019; Mori et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: MAIT and NKT cells have a restricted diversity, with an invariant TCRα chain and a constrained TCRβ repertoire, and are MR1- or CD1-restricted, respectively.
source: These have a restricted diversity, with an invariant TCRα chain and a constrained TCRβ repertoire, and are MR1- or CD1-restricted, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge about MAIT and NKT cells.

claim: The repertoire of polyspecific TCRs is highly diverse for both the TCR α and β chains, although with a specific usage of VDJ/VJ recombination.
source: In contrast, the repertoire of polyspecific TCRs is highly diverse for both the TCR αand β chains, although with a specific usage of VDJ/VJ recombination.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the data presented.

claim: Polyspecific T cells found in adults cannot be the remnant of fetal/neonatal T cells that have been described as having a promiscuous repertoire.
source: Also, polyspecific T cells found in adults cannot be the remnant of fetal/neonatal T cells that have been described as having a promiscuous repertoire, as these cells have repertoires enriched in germline-encoded TCRs (Rudd, 2020; Davenport et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: A recent study of multiple sclerosis pathogenesis identified autoreactive CD4+ T cell clones that can respond to self-peptides as well as peptides from EBV and from the bacteria Akkermansis muciniphila.
source: In the same line, a recent study of multiple sclerosis pathogenesis identified autoreactive CD4+ T cell clones that can respond to self-peptides as well as peptides from EBV and from the bacteria Akkermansis muciniphila (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to support the claim.

claim: In the T-scan platform setup experiment with CD8 cells activated by the NLV peptide from CMV pp65, while 25% of the T cells bind NLV tetramers, 2% of the T cells bind IE1 tetramers.
source: Actually, tetramer staining revealed that while 25% of the T cells in the NLV-expanded population bind NLV tetramers, 2% of the T cells bind IE1 tetramers (Kula et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to support the claim.

claim: The fold enrichment of the IE1-specific cells was close to that of NLV-specific cells (60 vs. 80, respectively) in the T-scan experiment.
source: Moreover, the fold enrichment of the IE1-specific cells was close to that of NLV-specific cells (60 vs. 80, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on data from the cited T-scan study.

claim: Activation with a single peptide results in a major expansion of cells with TCRs that can also respond to an unrelated peptide.
source: Thus, activation with a single peptide results in a major expansion of cells with TCRs that can also respond to an unrelated peptide.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the T-scan data.

claim: The fact that CMV, EBV, and influenza specificities are highly represented in polyspecific binding patterns likely reflects the biased representation of these specificities in the databases.
source: The fact that CMV, EBV, and influenza specificities are highly represented in polyspecific binding patterns likely reflects the biased representation of these specificities in the databases (15.9%, 16.2%, and 50.6%, respectively)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The detection of the diverse viral specificities of polyspecific T cells is largely underestimated due to the very low number of CDR3s with known viral specificities for viruses other than CMV, EBV, and influenza.
source: but also highlights that the detection of the diverse viral specificities of psT cells is largely underestimated due to the very low number of CDR3s with known viral specificities for viruses other than these.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the limitations.

claim: Polyspecific TCRs could represent at least 1/5 of the CD8 selected TCR repertoire.
source: Our results suggest that polyspecific TCRs could represent at least 1/5 of the CD8 selected TCR repertoire.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an estimate based on the data.

claim: The initial recruitment of frequent polyspecific effector T cells might be more efficient and rapid than having to rely on rare cells with stringent specificity that would need a period of expansion to provide enough fighters.
source: For life-threatening situations, the initial recruitment of frequent polyspecific effector T cells might be more efficient and rapid than having to rely on rare cells with stringent specificity that would need a period of expansion to provide enough fighters.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the functional role of polyspecific T cells.

claim: The early response of polyspecific T cells could provide some control of the viral spread that will allow time for the development of an immunologically fittest response to ensure the final control of the infection.
source: In the race between virus replication and the mounting of the immune response, this early response of polyspecific T cells could provide some control of the viral spread that will allow time for the development of an immunologically fittest response to ensure the final control of the infection.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the functional role of polyspecific T cells.

claim: Polyspecific T cells would explain how a very restricted repertoire of only about 1000 different TCRs arising from a single T-cell progenitor was sufficient to cope with viral infections in a child.
source: This would explain how a very restricted repertoire of only about 1000 different TCRs arising from a single T-cell progenitor was sufficient to cope with viral infections in a child (Bousso et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation with citation to support the example.

claim: Polyspecific T cells would explain why children vaccinated against measles in underdeveloped countries have a better life expectancy than unvaccinated ones, which could be linked to an overall better response to infections with other pathogens.
source: They would also explain why children vaccinated against measles in underdeveloped countries have a better life expectancy than unvaccinated ones (when excluding measles-related events), which could be linked to an overall better response to infections with other pathogens (Aaby et al., 2003; Aaby et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation with citations to support the observation.

claim: Polyspecific TCRs form a paratopic network, made of TCRs that have a high probability of generation and are positively selected during thymocyte differentiation.
source: Altogether, polyspecific TCRs form a paratopic network, made of TCRs that have a high probability of generation and are positively selected during thymocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the data.

claim: The properties of polyspecific TCRs indicate that these TCRs have been positively selected during evolution, further supporting their overall beneficial effects.
source: These properties indicate that these TCRs have been positively selected during evolution, further supporting their overall beneficial effects.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A fuzzy recognition by polyspecific TCRs would explain the so-called 'heterologous immunity' in which T-cell responses to one pathogen can have a major impact on the course and outcome of a subsequent infection with an unrelated pathogen.
source: A fuzzy recognition by polyspecific TCRs would explain the so-called 'heterologous immunity' (Welsh and Selin, 2002; Sewell, 2012) in which T-cell responses to one pathogen can have a major impact on the course and outcome of a subsequent infection with an unrelated pathogen (Furman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation with citations to support the concept.

claim: Individual histories of fuzzy immune responses may create patient-specific 'antigenic sins' that might be responsible for the diverse quality of immune responses to viruses, from unapparent infection to fulminant immunopathology.
source: We speculate that individual histories of fuzzy immune responses may thus create patient-specific 'antigenic sins' that might be responsible for the diverse quality of immune responses to viruses, from unapparent infection to fulminant immunopathology (Peteranderl et al., 2016; Bertoletti and Ferrari, 2016; Tay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation with citations to support the concept.

claim: The origin of many immune diseases should be sought in the repeated activation of polyspecific T cells.
source: We speculate that the origin of many immune diseases should be sought in the repeated activation of polyspecific T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation.

claim: Thirteen human thymus samples were obtained from organ donors undergoing surgery after approval by the Agence de Biomédecine and the Ministry of Research.
source: Thirteen human thymus samples were obtained from organ donors undergoing surgery (Department of Cardiac Surgery, Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital, France) after approval by the Agence de Biomédecine and the Ministry of Research.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The age of organ donors at the time of sampling ranged from 19 to 65 years old.
source: Their age at the time of sampling ranged from 19 to 65 years old.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The male-to-female sex ratio of organ donors was 2.6.
source: The male-to-female sex ratio was 2.6.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: TCR repertoire library preparation and sequencing were performed on 100 ng of RNA from each sample with the SMARTer Human TCR a/b Profiling Kit.
source: TCR repertoire library preparation and sequencing were performed has previously described (Barennes et al., 2021). Briefly, TCR alpha and beta libraries were prepared on 100 ng of RNA from each sample with the SMARTer Human TCR a/b Profiling Kit (Takarabio) following the provider's protocol.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section with citation.

claim: FASTQ raw data files were processed for TRA and TRB sequences annotation using MiXCR software (v2.1.10) with RNA-Seq parameters.
source: FASTQ raw data files were processed for TRA and TRB sequences annotation using MiXCR (Bolotin et al., 2015) software (v2.1.10) with RNA-Seq parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section with citation.

claim: When two sequences were similar under the defined threshold, LD>1 (i.e., at most one AA difference), they were connected and designated as 'clustered' nodes.
source: When two sequences were similar under the defined threshold, LD>1 (i.e., at most one AA difference), they were connected and designated as 'clustered' nodes.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: CDR3s with more than one AA difference from any other sequences are not connected and were designated as 'dispersed' nodes.
source: CDR3s with more than one AA difference from any other sequences are not connected and were designated as 'dispersed' nodes.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The generation probability (Pgen) of a sequence is inferred using the Olga algorithm, which is inferred by IGoR.
source: The generation probability (Pgen) of a sequence is inferred using the Olga (Sethna et al., 2019) algorithm, which is inferred by IGoR (Marcou et al., 2018), for Figure 1E and Figure 2B.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section with citations.

claim: A total of 5437 unique tetramer-associated βCDR3s were identified and used from curated databases.
source: Virus-associated βCDR3s were selected from the original data sets only when derived from a TCR of sorted CD8 T cells that were bound by a specific tetramer. A total of 5437 such unique tetramer-associated βCDR3s were identified and used.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The single-cell data set contains single-cell alpha/beta TCRs from 160,914 CD8+ T cells isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells from four healthy donors.
source: This data set contains single-cell alpha/beta TCRs from 160,914 CD8+ T cells isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from four healthy donors.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: There were 139,378 unambiguous TCRs (with only one α and one β chain) in the single-cell data set.
source: There were 139,378 unambiguous TCRs (with only one α and one β chain).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The threshold defining positive dextramer binding was set at UMI counts greater than 10 for any given dextramer.
source: We set the threshold defining positive binding at UMI counts greater than 10 for any given dextramer.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: 15,195 unique virus-specific TCRs with at least one binding were identified in the single-cell data set.
source: This identified 15,195 unique virus-specific TCRs with at least one binding.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.
